rows.explainer:
In 2023, we began investigating SMC outside the Sahel region as part of our work on grants supporting SMC in new geographies. Our initial recommendation  was to include a -20% downward adjustment to SMC effectiveness in settings outside the Sahel to account for the effects of high drug resistance in these areas. See a description of this initial work here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xqxzz91s0qIqnLMZmlm3fkWXdVOdOI5PK1xUqNt-Ou4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.hqxk4jmcd9ek

In 2024, we updated our analysis based on newly available evidence and a number of conversations with experts. This work led to us having a slightly more pessimistic view of SMC effectiveness outside the Sahel, which we account for with a -25% downward adjustment.

rows.explainer:
In 2023, we began investigating SMC outside the Sahel region as part of our work on grants supporting SMC in new geographies. Our initial recommendation was to include a -10% downward adjustment for the increased risk that we think SMC campaigns outside the Sahel may have on future resistance and therefore future effectiveness of both prevention and treatment drugs. This is larger than the adjustment we apply for Sahelian countries (-4%), where we believe current levels of resistance to SMC drugs are lower. See a description of this initial work here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xqxzz91s0qIqnLMZmlm3fkWXdVOdOI5PK1xUqNt-Ou4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.hqxk4jmcd9ek

Scenario 2: Global Fund and/or PMI would replace the grantee's costs
rows.explainer: The Global Fund currently supports SMC in Niassa province in Mozambique, but our understanding from conversations with stakeholders is that the government sees Nampula—as a high-burden province and Mozambique's largest—as the highest priority for SMC. We think that if we had decided not to fund Nampula, the Global Fund would likely have moved its Niassa funding to cover SMC in part of Nampula instead. We don’t think the Global Fund would have covered the full program in Nampula (which has around three times the target population of Niassa); our best guess is that they would have supported about 40% of it with the funding currently allocated to Niassa.

rows.explainer: Changed for consistency: GiveWell's sheet used 0.0033545 units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly here. The site values cash with one shared benchmark for every model (The cash benchmark, under Data), the same figure that turns this model's multiple of cash back into units of value: where the sheet divides by it to make its multiple, the benchmark cancels in our view, so our units of value are the sheet's before it divided by cash. The evaluator view keeps 0.0033545.

Units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly
rows.explainer: GiveWell reports this model's result in multiples of cash transfers. Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models. Older sheets used older moral weights; the multiple of cash is the comparable number across years. It is the site's shared cash benchmark (The cash benchmark, under Data), the one figure every model's multiple of cash is turned into units of value with.
